title: Permanent: sum over permutations vs Ryser's formula
problem_statement: Given an n x n matrix A of integers, compute its permanent perm(A) = sum over all permutations s of {0..n-1} of prod_i A[i][s(i)], exactly (as an unbounded integer). The permanent of the 0 x 0 matrix is 1.

input.size_measure: n^2 entries, small integers in the harness. Costs count arithmetic operations; intermediate values have at most n log2(2 n M) + 1 = O(n log(n M)) bits for entries bounded by M >= 1 in absolute value (PROOFS.md section 4; at most a few machine words at the tested sizes).

algorithms.name: sum over all permutations
algorithms.idea: Evaluate the definition directly: for each of the n! permutations, multiply the n selected entries and add.
algorithms.pseudocode: total = 0; for each permutation s: total += prod_i A[i][s(i)]
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * n!) arithmetic operations: exactly n * n! multiplications and n! additions for n >= 1 (PROOFS.md section 1); Theta(n * n!) time given the machine-model assumption on itertools.permutations (background; PROOFS.md section 1.3)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) (given the machine-model assumption on itertools.permutations, background)
algorithms.correctness: Definition of the permanent: every permutation is generated once (documented behaviour of itertools.permutations, background; PROOFS.md section 1).

algorithms.name: Ryser's formula with Gray-code ordering
algorithms.idea: Inclusion-exclusion over the set S of columns the rows may use: perm(A) = (-1)^n sum_S (-1)^|S| prod_i (sum_{j in S} A[i][j]). Visiting the subsets in Gray-code order changes one column per step, so the n row sums are updated in Theta(n).
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n 2^n) arithmetic operations: exactly (n + 1)(2^n - 1) additions and subtractions, n (2^n - 1) multiplications and 2^(n-1) + [n odd] negations for n >= 1 (PROOFS.md section 2)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2) (a transposed copy of A; Theta(n) working state)
algorithms.correctness: Formula: Ryser 1963; proof: PROOFS.md section 2. Expanding prod_i sum_{j in S} A[i][j] gives the sum, over all maps f from rows to S, of prod_i A[i][f(i)]. By inclusion-exclusion the alternating sum over S keeps exactly the maps whose image is all n columns, i.e. the permutations. The Gray-code order k XOR (k >> 1) visits every non-empty column set once.

relationship: Super-exponential -> single exponential: Theta(n * n!) vs Theta(n 2^n), an improvement that stays exponential (secondary T8). The V2 check is a runtime fit; the exact operation counts are proved in PROOFS.md and checked in tests/test_proofs_permanent.py. The primary tag T6 rests on the #P-completeness of the permanent, which is background (cited, not proved here).

sources.note: Background only: the documented behaviour (successive permutations, lexicographic order, n!/(n - r)! of them) and the 'roughly equivalent' Python code, read on 2026-10-07.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree for n = 0..8 (the permutation sum is capped at n = 8) on random 0/1 matrices and on matrices with entries in [-2, 3]; Ryser alone is also run at n = 10, 12, 15. harness.check is independent of both: for n <= 12 it compares with an exact O(n 2^n) DP over column subsets (a third algorithm, no inclusion-exclusion), and for every n it checks perm(A) = det(A) mod 2 with a GF(2) elimination. tests/test_proofs_permanent.py checks perm(J_n) = n! and the derangement numbers perm(J_n - I) (both implementations for n = 0..8, Ryser for n = 0..12) and the exact operation counts of PROOFS.md. V2: runtimes fitted against n * n! and n 2^n on matrices with entries in [1, 4].

caveats: The primary tag T6 rests on background (see below), and T8 on the pair itself, a super-polynomial -> faster super-polynomial improvement (PROOFS.md section 3). The operation counts treat integer arithmetic as unit cost; the integers involved have at most n log2(2 n M) + 1 = O(n log(n M)) bits (PROOFS.md section 4), which adds at most a small polynomial factor in bit complexity.
notes: Contrast with determinant-cofactor-vs-gaussian: the determinant is the same sum with signs sgn(s), and over a field Gaussian elimination computes it with O(n^3) field operations (proved in that entry). Mod 2 the signs vanish (-1 = 1), so perm(A) mod 2 = det(A) mod 2, which elimination over GF(2) computes (PROOFS.md section 5); the exact integer value is the hard part. Approximation and BosonSampling are listed under background.

background.statement: Computing the permanent is #P-complete, even for 0/1 matrices, so a polynomial-time algorithm would give FP = #P and in particular P = NP. This is the reason for the primary tag T6: no polynomial algorithm is known or expected.
Glynn's formula gives the same Theta(n 2^n) operation count as Ryser's.

For matrices with non-negative entries a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme exists. It approximates, it does not compute exactly, and it does not cover matrices with negative or complex entries.

BosonSampling, a proposed quantum-advantage experiment, samples photon output patterns of a linear-optical network whose probabilities are squared absolute values of permanents of submatrices of the network's unitary. Efficient exact classical sampling would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, and approximate sampling is argued to be hard under further conjectures. BosonSampling samples from this distribution; it does not compute permanents, so it gives no quantum algorithm for this problem.

Machine-model assumption of this entry: CPython's itertools.permutations(range(n)) behaves as its documented 'roughly equivalent' Python code. It yields every permutation of range(n) exactly once, as n-tuples in lexicographic order (documented behaviour); it does O(n * n!) work in total over the n! permutations, that is amortised O(n) per permutation, while a single step can take Theta(n^2); and it keeps O(n) words of state. PROOFS.md section 0.1 proves the two cost properties for the documented code; that the C implementation has the same costs is assumed, not proved.
